title: The Global Polycrisis Outlook 2027
subtitle: Mapping the Convergence of Climate, Pollution, Resource, Demographic, and Governance Risks in an Increasingly Interconnected World
dek: Why 2027 is the year the slow variables and the fast shocks arrive together, and what that means for those who must prepare.
abstract: The risks that researchers have long treated as separate problems are arriving together. In 2026 the world is on course for its first- or second-warmest year on record while a very strong El Niño builds toward a December peak; a war in the Gulf has halted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and produced what the International Energy Agency calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market; the FAO Food Price Index has risen for three straight months to its highest level since November 2022; official development assistance fell by 23 per cent in 2025, the largest one-year drop on record; and a Bundibugyo-virus Ebola outbreak with no licensed vaccine is spreading through a conflict zone in eastern Congo. This report asks what that convergence means for 2027, and how to think about it clearly.

The report organises the evidence into five risk clusters, climate, pollution, resource, demographic and governance, and three coupling pathways from the polycrisis literature: common stresses, domino effects and inter-systemic feedbacks. It finds that the clusters are unequal in the pressure they transmit. A transparent coupling assessment (Figure 13) ranks resource systems and governance as the strongest transmitters of stress, and resource and demographic systems as the strongest receivers. The binding vulnerability in 2027 is therefore not any single hazard but the thinning of the buffers, aid, fiscal space, grain reserves, health capacity and diplomatic trust, that normally stop a hazard becoming a crisis. The report maps nine regional convergence hotspots, led by the Sahel, the Horn of Africa and Sudan, South Asia and the Middle East, and sets out four scenarios for 2027 defined by two swing factors: whether the Gulf energy shock resolves, and how severe the El Niño impacts prove.

The outlook is serious but not fatalistic. Global hunger fell for a third consecutive year in 2025, clean energy investment ($2.2 trillion) is nearly double fossil investment ($1.2 trillion), and wind and solar met 99 per cent of the growth in global electricity demand in 2025. The report closes with priorities by actor, a monitoring dashboard with explicit trigger thresholds, and a 2027 calendar of decision points. Its central conclusion is that the cheapest response to a convergence of risks is to protect the buffers before the shocks land.

method: This report synthesises 2025-26 publications from the WMO, NOAA, Copernicus, UNEP, IEA, FAO, WFP, FEWS NET, WHO, UNHCR, IDMC, OECD, UNCTAD, IMF, World Bank, SIPRI, UCDP, V-Dem and the World Economic Forum, together with peer-reviewed literature on crisis entanglement. Every quantitative claim is linked inline to its source. Figures 2-12 chart values reported by cited sources (with derivations noted); Figures 1, 14 and 16-17 are conceptual or calendar graphics; Figures 13 and 15 are author assessments on a transparent 0-3 scale and are labelled as such. Information is current to 9 October 2026; several events discussed (the El Niño peak, COP31, the IMF October outlook) have not yet occurred.
